Here's the migration plan analysis:

ENDPOINTS & BEHAVIOR:
1. GET /health - Returns {"status": "ok"} (200)
2. GET /users/<user_id> - Returns user JSON or 404
3. GET /products - Filterable list with q/category params, returns {"count": N, "items": [...]}
4. POST /login - Requires user_id in body, sets session, returns 401 on failure
5. GET /me - Session-protected user info (401 if no session)
6. GET /admin - Admin-only endpoint (403 for non-admins)
7. GET /old-home - Redirects to /health (302)

SESSION & AUTH:
- Uses Flask sessions with secret_key
- Session stores user_id as integer
- /me and /admin require authentication
- /admin additionally requires role="admin"

DATA ACCESS:
- In-memory USERS dictionary (keyed by string IDs)
- In-memory PRODUCTS list
- User lookups by string ID
- Product filtering by name/category

MODULE RESPONSIBILITIES:
1. app.py - Flask app creation, config, and startup
2. routes.py - Route definitions and request handling
3. services.py - Business logic (auth, product filtering)
4. repository.py - Data access (users/products CRUD)

MIGRATION NOTES:
- Must preserve all status codes and JSON structures
- Session behavior must remain identical
- Authorization checks must stay at same strictness level
- Redirect (/old-home) must maintain 302 status
- Port 5056 must be maintained
- Secret key must remain the same

The modernization will maintain identical external behavior while improving code organization. No security reductions will be made. The application will continue to run with `python app.py` on port 5056.
